commit.message:
Effect interface update

This updates the effects to the form my microcontroller project is
currently using:

 - move the effects headers into a 'audio' subdirectory

 - use a more complete 'struct effect' model with pot descriptors

 - updated and extended math helper routines

This updates a few core effects, brings a few others in from the
microcontroller code (boost / pitch), and removes some others that were
either pointless (fm/am signal generation) or didn't sound great or
weren't very educational (pll / growlingbass / distortion / tube).

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add "chasing tone" effect

All great guitarists have at some point wondered "what would it sound
like if I was accompanied by a scurry of insane chipmunks - with tiny
tiny bagpipes?"

Jimi Hendrix wondered.  The closest he ever came was the Roger Mayer
Octavia together with the Univox Uni-Vibe, and he turned to drugs to
fill that empty spot in his soul from never having found that perfect
tone.

And Plato spent five years in a cave - it wasn't an allegory - together
with a family of chipmunks, trying to teach them to play the bagpipes in
order to find true knowledge and understanding.  He too failed in his
search for that perfect tone, and ended up giving up on electric guitar
entirely.  Today known mainly for his philosophy, with few sources even
mentioning his bloody hands from trying to sew tiny tiny bagpipes.

Wonder no more.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

growlingbass: fix abs() confusion, use fabsf()

I've made the mistake of using abs instead of fabs, here is a quick fix.

[ Updated to fix both places, and also to use 'fabsf()' which is the
  proper one that avoids double conversions - not relevant on a real
  computer, but visible on microcontrollers with hardware support only
  for 32-bit floats  - Linus ]

Signed-off-by: Philippe Strauss <catseyechandra@proton.me>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

warn about implicit floating point to integer conversions

This got disabled when I had to disable '-Wdouble-promotion' due to it
being practically unavoidable with variadic functions.

But while '-Wdouble-promotion' wasn't practical, I should have kept
'-Wfloat-conversion' around.

Yes, it requires a few manual casts for out hacky 'pow()' usage that
I'll need to fix for the actual real-time microcontroller case, but
those are good to have anyway, not the unavoidable issue with the
calling conventions.

That makes a couple of bugs in the growlingbass implementation obvious.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add 'growlingbass' effect

A growling/purring bass effect with a sign flip one period over two for
subharmonic generation and split odd/even order distorsion.

Simpler than what has been discussed on github repos and very effective.

Signed-off-by: Philippe Strauss <catseyechandra@proton.me>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add random 'tube' model

It's broken and has only a very fleeting association with anything that
would be a tube, but I'm committing it just as an example and 'something
like this'.  I'm pretty sure I'm doing very wrong things with the FIR
filter, but it works (modulo that random multiplier hack) with at least
one amplifier impulse file (converted to raw format).

And when I say "works", I mean "makes something that sounds like
guitar".  I'm not sure the sound actually matches what it should sound
like, and how much that FIR thing really matters.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

convert: add somewhat realtime control interface

This is pretty raw and stupid, but I wanted to try changing the
conversion parameters on the fly with a "control file descriptor".

This is currently very limited, and doesn't have an interface for
switching the effect itself at runtime (like I do on the hardware:
long-press the foot-switch for one second), but at least allows for
sending "pot commands" to change the pot values dynamically.

The format is a five-byte ASCII packet of 'pXYY\n', which sets put X to
value YY (X being in the range '0'..'3', and YY being '00'..'99').

Why that format? Because right now the only testing I've done is from
the terminal, doing something like this:

    $ ./convert --control=0 phaser input.raw |
                aplay -c1 -r 48000 -f s32 -B 100

and then you can just type in those commands at the terminal by hand:
the "--control=0" is the magic that says that fd 0 is a control channel.

Very combersome, very stupid, but hey, it works.

Note that I'm back to using 'aplay' for this, because with ffplay the
latency is absolutely horrible.  Something like three seconds of audio
later does any pot command take effect, because ffplay has slurped in a
lot of data into its input buffers.

In contrast, with 'aplay', the effect is basically instantaneous,
particularly with that "-B 100" that keeps the buffering to a very
reasonable 100ms.

If there is a flag for ffplay that makes it not buffer input very much,
I haven't found it (and yes, I tried the obvious ones, but no, I didn't
do any exhaustive search since aplay works fine for me).

It should be very possible to wrap a UI around this, and I should also
add some command to switch the effect at runtime too.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

convert: start parsing arguments more flexibly

In particular, allow default pot values (all at noon), and specifying
input and output files rather than always doing stdin/stdout.

And no, this is still not all that smart, but it is at least a tiny bit
more flexible than it used to be, and the Makefile has been updated
accordingly.

Also, when F_SETPIPE_SZ is available, use it to limit the buffering of
the output if it's a pipe.  That, together with the very limited
buffering by 'make_one_noise()' should make this somewhat real-time if
the target i sreading a pipe and doesn't have huge input buffers.

Put another way: if I add interfaces to modify the pots concurrently,
that hopefully actually takes effect in a timely way.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Update effect definition interface

Add a 'description' callback for printing pot meaning, and pass the pot
values as an array to it and to the init function.

This makes the interface a bit cleaner, but also means that we can now
use the same structure as the RP2354A hardware does: call the '->init'
function multiple times as the pots may change during playback.

The pots don't actually change during playback - yet - but this starts
the restructuring.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Refactor visualize.py to use native sample units and improve slider

Dynamically visualize the X axis in different modes, making the raw
sample data the core internal data.  This is similar to how we format
the Y axis.

 - Switch internal logic (view updates, data loading, panning) from
   seconds to sample indices (integers) to match the underlying data
   structure

 - Add 'Samples' vs 'Time' X-axis mode toggle using RadioButtons

 - Update X-axis FuncFormatter to display either integer samples or
   seconds based on selected mode

 - Overhaul slider logic to dynamically switch ranges and formats:
    - In Time mode: Range [0, Duration Seconds], Format '%.3f s'
    - In Samples mode: Range [0, Max Samples], Format '%d'

 - Make the slider be a range slider rather than just showing where the
   current audio window plot starts

This was more antigravity with hand-holding and some manual edits.

Also just update the initial window size to the full audio size (ok,
still limited to one hour), since it's now no longer a performance issue
at least with the test file I have.  Knock wood.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Optimize visualize.py for large datasets

Speed up plotting (courtesy of antigravity) to the point where you can
reasonably zoom out to fairly long audio files:

 - Implement downsampling based on MAX_PLOT_POINTS to avoid
   over-plotting massive datasets

 - Pre-allocate time axis and index buffers to eliminate transient
   float allocations during zoom/scroll operations

 - Use in-place numpy operations for coordinate generation

 - Remove arbitrary MAX_WIDTH_SEC limit and instead clamp zoom
   to the actual data duration

 - Fix backwards compatibility issue with np.linspace by using
   np.copyto and a pre-computed index buffer

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

tests: clean up naming and update gitignore file

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Get rid of too random "helper" functions, tweak pot behavior

Let's avoid the fastpow() helpers as much as possible, because they end
up acting too randomly outside their proper ranges.

I'll have to come up with something better for actual hardware, but for
now, let's pretend that we have a good "pow2()" function, and make it do
the exact thing for simulation for now.

And for frequencies, where we don't want a linear function (because
human hearing response is basically logarithmic) let's use a helper
macro that gives reasonable values: 220Hz to 6.5kHz with the pot
centered giving exactly 1kHz.  A simple cubic function gives a somewhat
reasonable curve.

This all makes the pot values much less random.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add verification of fastsincos() results

Since I noticed I had gotten the cos part wrong, let's just make sure it
doesn't happen again.

Also a good idea to verify the conversion to fixed point.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix the 'cos' part of fastsincos

The linear interpolation was just broken, and I had never noticed.  It
interpolates between the wrong indexes when it reverses the phase for
the cosine part.  I had tested the code, but the errors were small
enough to not be glaringly obvious because this is all just "fix the
values in between the table lookup entries".

Fixing it takes the max error down from 4.5 digits to 5.3 digits (so
accuracy goes from about 15 to about 18 bits), and _maybe_ that might
show in some instability in the biquad calculations, but it's likely all
entirely in the noise.

Noticed not because of any numerical errors, but when going "Hmm" when
converting this all to pure fixed point math.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix bad phaser pot ranges

The phaser pot ranges were bad, and resulted in attempting a max
frequency of 100kHz at the extreme range, which obviously doesn't work
at all for audio.  It was a combination of "extreme octave range for
testing on a noisy airplane" and just not thinking too much about the
center frequency in the first place.

Make the pot ranges less crazy.  They are still entirely arbitrary, but
at least the extreme frequencies should now be within the audio range.

Fixes #59

Reported-by: Akihiko Shirai (@kaitas)
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Update visualize.py: use raw int32 data, just scale the Y axis

Not only should this be more efficient by not unnecessarily converting
the underlying data, but it makes it easy to visualize the data any
which way you want.

Add a radio button to pick between "Raw" data (hex representation),
"Scaled" (the -1 ..  1 floating point range that we use interally) or
"Volt" (for an approximation of the actual signal level voltage).

The "Volt" mode is now the default, and assumes that the signal we're
viewing is basically a line level signal at 1 Vrms (aka "0 dBV").
That's what the TAC5112 unbalanced full-range input is (and my signal
generator and oscilloscope agrees).

[ This was a mix of Google Antigravity and me ]

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Clean up integer type system a bit, and prep for extensions

I had started out using 'uint' because that came from the pico sdk and
seemed to be common there, but it's a horrible type that doesn't really
specify the size and is just a lazy form of the standard types.

And for historical reasons I despise 'uint32_t' and friends: it may be
universal now, but it used to be one of those things where system
headers didn't reliably have them, so you ended up with #ifdef's to do
your own versions anyway, and it was all just unnecessarily painful.

So I'm ornery, but I'm used to the kernel types that are nice and short
and simple: 'u32' and friends.  Let's just use them.

And because the target hardware (RP2354A with dual Cortex-M33 cores)
should have a fast 32x32->64 integer multiply with accumulate, I'm
considering doing some fixed-point ops in paths where the 32-bit floats
aren't necessary, and would avoid the type conversion overheads.

So I'm adding the s64/u64 types too in preparation for that.  It's
possible that I should just do all of the LFO as 32-bit fractional
integers (it already largely is).

Maybe even use fixed-point for the biquad code, which is what the
TAC5112 does internally.  That would give higher precision than using
floats thanks to a bigger mantissa, but with the caveat that the range
would be very limited and would require a lot of care.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add first cut at some noise gate logic

It's hardcoded in order to not depend on pots that are then used for the
real effects.

Put another way: this is more a conceptual thing that a real proper
noise gate.  But I have ported this to the RP2354A board and tested it
on real hardware with a guitar, and it doesn't cause popping for me and
does do something.

But that's obviously because it's been tuned for that setup, so YMMV.
Popping noises were definitely heard with an earlier broken approach.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Abstract out the initial and final integer sample processing

This is partly just to clean the code up, but partly to also do the
signal magnitude processing independently of the 'magnitude' effect, and
do it using cheap integer operations at the initial sample processing
stage.

The reason for that is that I'll do at least a noise gate.  Maybe a
compressor.

[ NOTE! This decay is intentionally much more aggressive than the
  previous random decay was, so the 'magnitude' effect is *not*
  identical to the old one.

  Both old and new decays are just random values, they don't have any
  real meaning, this new 60ms one was what I picked when I was testing
  some noise gating. The noise gate part I'm still thinking about ]

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add a distortion/overdrive effect with clipping modes and tone control

Parameters:

 - pot1: drive/gain (1x - 50x)
 - pot2: tone filter cutoff (1kHz - 10kHz)
 - pot3: output level (0 - 100%)
 - pot4: mode (0-0.33 = soft, 0.33-0.66 = hard, 0.66-1 = asymmetric)

Uses the existing biquad LPF for tone control.  Asymmetric mode
approximates tube-amp even-harmonic distortion.

Signed-off-by: The Hand <nikolaiflaukowski@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix flanger debug output printing wrong values

Both the delay and feedback printouts were wrong due to excessive
cut-and-paste and some random changes over time.

@NickFlach reported the feedback case, but apparently missed that
the delay value printout was also wrong ;)

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Don't use the "canonical" biquad direct form 2

It may be canonical, and use less state, but testing does seem to show
that the floating point instability is a very real issue.  When testing
a low-pass filter on some loads, DF2 caused nasty extra noise.

Maybe there are mitigations for it, but since DF1 worked better for the
phaser too, let's just give up entirely on supporting both forms and
purely use DF1.  It's not really noticeably more expensive, and clearly
behaves better.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix final float -> int conversion overflow

The final conversion from float to s32 does

	sample = (int)(out * 0x80000000);

and that overflows for 1.0, turning it into the most negative integer
number.

I could just make the thing multiply by 0x7ffffffff instead, and miss
out on turning -1 to that most negative number, but I think the best
model is to just explicitly check for overflow by testing the sign of
the float vs the resulting integer.

That deals with any small overflow outside the [-1,1] range too, which
allows the effects to be a bit lazy if they want to (although gross
overflow could then result in the sign overflowing "twice" and not be
caught, so effects shouldn't be *too* lazy).

This may explain some crackling in anything that ended up doing the full
FP range (although you really should try to avoid that anyway).

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add LFO sinewave verification test

It's slow, so don't run it unless you change the implementation.  It
single-steps the LFO, so a cycle is the full 2**32 steps, and checks out
sinewave approximation against the proper math.h sin() values.

The 256-entry lookup table with linear interpolation is good to about 16
bits of precision.  None of the users really care about it being a
perfect sinusoid, so that's more than good enough.  But let's at least
verify it.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add amplitude-modulation signal generator

This is exactly the same as the fm effect, just for amplitude modulation
instead.  And like the fm effect, it ignores its input and just acts as
a signal generator, mainly to generate test-cases for other effects.

[ Side note: I think I've successfully picked a super-annoying AM sound.
  Making dissonant sounds seems to be my super power ]

Put another way: this is useless, except I'm still thinking about doing
a noise gate / compressor thing, and I want to have an input signal for
that.

Plus I'm reading a paper [1] about spice models for vacuum tube
amplifiers, and am possibly considering some kind of vacuum tube pre-amp
emulation thing.  Ridiculous, I know, but that's kind of the point of
this whole project.  I'm not doing this for any *sane* reasons.

Link: https://leachlegacy.ece.gatech.edu/papers/tubeamp/tubeamp.pdf [1]
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix 'discont' effect potentiometer behavior

I messed up when I imported the discont effect from the RP2354A code: I
had gone back-and-forth in that repo on just how much you could change
the pitch, alternating between "arbitrary", "by semitones" and "fixed to
fourths, fifths and octaves".

When I then moved the code over to this simulation repo, I decided to go
back to "arbitrary", and that people could just make the pot value
negative, so that you could just go down an octave by doing

    ./discont -1 ....

That was technically true, but it means that now if I want to test
things on the RP2354A hardware after being happy with it in simulation,
I'll always have to mess with this potentiometer mapping.

So go back to the assumption that the pot values should primarily be
floating point values in the range [0,1], and that 0 means "one octave
down" and 1 means "one octave up" (approximately, because we're using
that quick-and-dirty very inexact fastpow2_m1() function).

So now it takes the pot value, and multiplies it by two and subtracts
one to get the "power of two". Thus turning [0,1] into [-1,1].

In simulations, you can still use negative values if you want, so that
(if we had a better 'pow2()' approximation) you could do

    ./discont -0.5 ...

to go down two octaves, or use '2' to go up three octaves).

The actual pitch shifting does actually work for those kinds of ranges,
but fastpow2_m1() does not, so currently a pot value outside 0..1 gives
pretty nonsensical actual step values.  Replace 'fastpow2_m1(x)' with
'pow(2.0,x)-1' if you want to play silly games with a silly effect.

[ And again, just to clarify: the "pitch shifting" of the discont.h
  effect is really not anything like a real pitch shift. It's walking
  the delay line at non-unity speeds to speed up or slow down the
  signal, and then abruptly jumping back or forward to catch up to real
  time.

  It then tries to hide those discontinuities from the jumping around by
  using two different delays and mixing them together with the
  discontinuity points faded away, which is why the effect is called
  "discont" ]

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Use ffplay instead of aplay, and allow python override

'aplay' may be the simple - and very traditional and old - way to play
audio files on Linux, but if you are on some other platform it's
apparently odd.  Fair enough.

So let's use 'ffplay' by default instead, since we already use 'ffmpeg'
for the format conversion.  It may be a more complex command line, but
it's related to the tool we already use.

For similar reasons, make the python interpreter a variable that can be
easily overridden.

Reported-by: @zeelsheladiya
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix math library linking causing link errors for 'gensin'

The Makefile used LDFLAGS to set "-lm" to link in the math library for
the 'sin()' function use in gensin.c.  That is wrong, and causes the
'-lm' to be too early in the implicit executable rule, resulting in
potentially undefined references at link time.

It just happened to work for me even with the wrong placement of the
linker flag.  The reason is simply that my build environment used
dynamic linking for the math library, which brings in all of libm.so
regardless of what functions you use.

A static link that only brings in the actually used functions would then
not have seen the use of 'sin()' (yet) and then the wrong placement
causes

    gensin.c: undefined reference to `sin'

Fix it by using the proper Makefile variable for the math library:
LDLIBS.

Reported-by: Max McEvoy <maxmcevoy@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Thomas <thomas.blakely@gmx.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
